questions.problems: The question answers itself: slow-wave sleep is named in the passage, so the item is pure recall of 'slow-wave = delta'; B (spindles and K-complexes, stage N2) is the only distractor with any pull.
D is the only option that randomizes or manipulates anything, so a student who knows 'causation needs manipulation' spots it at once; A, B and C are weak.
A restates the table almost word for word, and B, C and D each make an obvious causal leap; B is also contradicted by the design, since stress came after learning to criterion.
D (parasympathetic) is too weak to tempt anyone; B (adrenal medulla) is the only real trap.

questions.ambiguity: B: some students will see 'lower-income neighborhoods' and pick residential segregation, though segregation describes where groups live, not unequal access to resources.

questions.problems: C is factually false (self-rated health predicts later illness and death), so it is not a usable objection; A is easy to dismiss with 600 respondents per quartile.
The stem's wording ('more economic and political power ... benefit wealthier residents') points straight at conflict theory.
The stem's clause 'long-term residents who stayed report no change' largely gives the answer away; A (rising rents raise tenants' incomes) is implausible enough that no one would pick it.

questions.ambiguity: B: a late arrival is a failure that she blames on an outside cause, which is also self-serving bias; only the phrase 'contrast between her two explanations' tips it to actor-observer.
questions.problems: Because both B and C fit, the item depends on one cue word; a version where the nurse's own outcome is not a failure would separate the two answers cleanly.

questions.ambiguity: B: teachers' low expectations shaping a student is the classic Pygmalion/self-fulfilling-prophecy setup, though the outcome asked about is self-concept, not performance.
questions.problems: Pygmalion normally means high expectations raising performance; here the expectations are low (a Golem effect), which may confuse students who choose B.

questions.ambiguity: A: role strain is the standard trap, but it describes demands within one role, while here two roles clash.

overall: The set reads like real MCAT Psych/Soc material: the passages are realistic and internally consistent (the nap subgroups average 18x84 + 12x69 = 78%, matching Table 1; the cortisol timing fits a Trier-style stressor), and the topics are squarely on the AAMC content outline. Its strongest items are the reasoning ones (P1-2, P1-6, P2-3, P2-6) and the clean term-application items (S6, S7, S8, P2-1). Its weakest point is difficulty. Most items are EASY, with several stems that telegraph the answer (P1-1, P2-4, P2-6) and some throwaway distractors (P1-4 D, P2-6 A, P2-3 C, which is false). S3 and S5 each have a defensible second answer (self-serving bias; Pygmalion) that rests on fine wording, which is MCAT-typical but worth tightening.
